summary: Defines two SIP header fields, Resource-Priority and Accept-Resource-Priority, for communicating resource priority. They can influence how SIP user agents, such as gateways and IP phones, and SIP proxies behave, but not how IP routers forward packets. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4412 adds SIP headers that let a request ask for priority when phone systems or gateways are short of capacity. A receiving system checks whether the requester is allowed to use that priority, then may serve the request first, wait it in a priority queue, or reject it.

subtitle: SIP headers that request prioritized access to scarce call-handling resources.

tldr.problem: During emergencies, SIP gateways, proxies and receiving devices may lack capacity. SIP had no request header for asking an element to prioritize access to those resources.
tldr.mechanism: Resource-Priority carries registered namespace and priority values, while Accept-Resource-Priority lists values a server is willing to process. After authorization, an element can preempt a lower-priority session or queue the request.
tldr.outcome: The extension can affect SIP elements but does not directly change IP router forwarding. RFC 4412 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7134.

today: RFC 4412 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7134. The unit metadata does not list an RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Need for Resource Priority
sections.content:
During emergencies, telephone circuits, gateways, receiving devices and SIP proxies can become congested. RFC 4412 defines a way for SIP requests to ask for prioritized access to those resources. IP network resources are outside the scope of SIP signaling in this specification.

The new Resource-Priority header differs from SIP's Priority header. Priority describes importance to the human recipient; Resource-Priority can affect access to gateways, proxies and end systems, and its values are subject to authorization.

Systems that do not understand the extension can ignore its header and continue normal SIP processing unless the request requires the extension. The header does not itself change how IP routers forward packets.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 4412 lets a SIP request ask for priority when call-handling resources are scarce. This priority is different from a message saying that a call matters to its human recipient.

sections.title: The Priority Headers
sections.content:
A Resource-Priority request header contains values in the form namespace.priority, such as dsn.flash. Namespaces and priority values are case-insensitive ASCII tokens without periods, and their definitions must be registered with IANA.

A request can carry values from different namespaces, but it must not repeat a namespace in the same SIP message. Values can appear in one comma-separated header or in several headers; their order has no significance.

The Accept-Resource-Priority response header lists values a user agent server is willing to process. It does not promise that enough resources are available. The resource-priority option tag can appear in Require and Supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A priority value combines the name of a priority system with one level from that system. A response can list which values the server understands, but that list does not guarantee a call will succeed.

sections.title: How SIP Elements Handle Requests
sections.content:
An element first checks whether it recognizes a namespace. If it recognizes none, it treats the request as having no Resource-Priority header. Otherwise, it checks local authorization policy; an unauthorized request is rejected. An authorized request proceeds normally when resources are available.

When resources are scarce, an element may preempt an existing lower-priority session or place the request in a priority queue. One higher-priority session may displace several lower-priority sessions; equal-priority requests are not preempted by default. Proxies do not manage sessions and therefore do not perform session preemption.

Queues generally serve requests first-come, first-served within each priority, selecting from the highest-priority non-empty queue. A full queue rejects a new request. A server can impose a waiting-time limit and return 408 when that limit expires; a user agent server should send 182 (Queued) while a request waits.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP system checks whether it recognizes the priority and whether local rules allow the requester to use it. If capacity is short, the system can end a lower-priority session or make the request wait behind other requests of the same priority.

sections.title: Responses to Failed Requests
sections.content:
An unknown priority value is normally treated as if no priority header were present, and the value must not be changed or deleted. If the request includes Require: resource-priority, an element that does not understand the value must return 417 (Unknown Resource-Priority); it may list acceptable values in its response.

An unauthenticated requester receives 401 or 407, while an authenticated but unauthorized requester receives 403. If an authorized request cannot be served because signaling capacity is insufficient, the response is 503. Insufficient media or gateway capacity can produce 488.

A busy user agent server returns 486 when the request has priority equal to or below all active calls. Requests that time out in a queue receive 408. These different responses identify whether the problem is an unknown value, identity, permission or available capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Different failures have different responses. A system can say it does not know the value, cannot verify or authorize the caller, or has no capacity to handle the request.

sections.title: Priority Namespaces
sections.content:
A request may contain values from multiple namespaces because a call can cross administrative domains with different priority systems. An element that understands more than one namespace must define a local total ordering while preserving the priority order within each namespace. The RFC recommends using a consistent ordering throughout an administrative domain.

RFC 4412 registers five namespaces. DSN has five levels and uses preemption; DRSN has six levels and uses preemption; Q735 has five levels and uses preemption; ETS and WPS each have five levels and use priority queues. DRSN's highest value, flash-override-override, can preempt another request at the same value.

A new namespace must be defined in a Standards Track RFC and provide a finite list of priority levels and its intended algorithm. Organizations are encouraged to reuse existing namespaces when they meet their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Different organizations can use different named priority systems. A system that understands several must decide how to compare them while keeping each system's own ranking intact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Abusing priority can deny service to other users, take over gateway capacity or terminate existing calls. Systems are therefore expected to authenticate and authorize requests carrying the Resource-Priority header, including requests from users inside the same administrative domain.

Supporting user agents and proxies must implement SIP over TLS, the sips URI scheme and Digest authentication. User agents should also implement S/MIME. Proxies may need to inspect or modify Resource-Priority, so a sender that wants proxies to act on it must also place it in the outer SIP message when S/MIME is used.

The RFC expects denial-of-service attacks during emergencies. It directs systems to limit the state, computation and network resources that an unauthorized user can cause them to consume.
sections.plainLanguage: A false priority request could take resources away from other callers, so systems must check identity and permission. They must also limit the work an unauthorized request can make them perform.
